Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a 19-year-old male with stalking trauma, body-focused shame is hard to reconcile unless there was physical or sexual assault. With the given trauma type, this item is clinically incongruent and stands out from the other appraisal items, which are otherwise plausible for stalking.

issues.item: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless the stalker was also a trusted person. Because trauma type has already been fixed as stalking and no other node supplies context supporting an intimate or trusted-perpetrator stalking scenario, this item is clinically questionable in this profile.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' can fit only if the stalker was a trusted person, but the profile gives no other items in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies to support an interpersonal-betrayal formulation. Paired with global characterological self-blame, this creates a specific relational-trauma narrative that is not otherwise represented in the self-report.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a stalking trauma, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is not impossible, but it implies the stalker was a trusted close other. The rest of the profile provides no supporting items in Memory, Threat, Triggers, or Strategies, and with no active formulation edges this appraisal stands as an unsupported trauma-specific claim. The other appraisal items ('I have to be on guard all the time', 'The world is a dangerous place') fit stalking more generically, but the betrayal item makes the node less coherent as a standalone set.

issues.item: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time
issues.explanation: These two items are not negative appraisals in the usual cognitive sense; they describe ongoing threat monitoring/safety behavior rather than evaluative beliefs. With a formulation showing no active edges and only the Negative Appraisals node populated, selecting predominantly hypervigilance/vigilance items makes the node content misaligned with the intended construct.

vignette:
Kwame is a nineteen-year-old UX designer from a Ghanaian-American family, living alone in a studio apartment in a midwestern city. Eight months ago, during his first year of college, a former classmate began leaving him voice notes, texts from unknown numbers, and showing up at the library where he studied. The messages started as ambiguous compliments and shifted over weeks into threats: "I see where you go," "You don't get to ignore me." One night he found the man standing outside his dormitory window, just watching. The police were called, a restraining order was filed, and the classmate was eventually arrested, but the case did not go to trial. Kwame transferred to an online program and took a remote UX internship to avoid campus entirely.

The world feels different now. Every time he unlocks his phone or hears a notification chime, a cold pinch runs through his chest. He has become certain that danger is continuous and invisible, that the real threat was never a single person but a world that lets such things happen without consequence. He scans crowds for familiar faces, checks the rearview mirror three times before turning into his apartment complex, and never listens to music on his headphones when he walks to the grocery store, because he needs to hear everything. This constant scanning is not a choice; it is simply what his body does now, a low hum of alertness that has become his baseline.

Kwame also blames himself for what happened. In the weeks after the stalking began, he kept replaying the early interactions-the casual conversations at a student orientation event, the friendly wave he returned, the moment he gave the classmate his phone number to coordinate a group project. He has come to believe that if he had been more distant, more guarded, less polite, the whole ordeal could have been avoided. This self-blame loops quietly in his mind, separate from the hypervigilance, a private conviction that he is responsible for having been targeted.

His work as a UX designer-usually a source of focus and pride-has become a minefield. His desk faces the window, and he cannot concentrate because movements in the peripheral reflection yank his attention. He now sits with his back to the wall in every coffee shop used for coworking, and he has stopped attending team meetups altogether, claiming scheduling conflicts. His manager has noticed a drop in responsiveness to Slack messages and a reluctance to join video calls with more than two people. Kwame knows this is hurting his standing, but what frightens him most is the thought that his stalker could simply be using a different name, starting over, and that no amount of caution will protect him.

He finally scheduled an intake appointment after a weekend panic attack triggered by a casual encounter: a stranger on the elevator smiled and said, "I've seen you around." Kwame spent the next two hours locked in his bathroom, convinced that the stalking had begun again. His roommate from the previous semester, the only person who knew the full story, had stopped returning his calls months ago, tired of the constant check-ins and the refusal to go out. Kwame arrives at the clinic hoping for strategies to feel safe again, but underneath that hope is the fear that safety is no longer something the world can offer him.
